# iref - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iref/4.1.0/iref/index.html

## Expand description

This crates provides an implementation of
[Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs, aka URLs)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier) and [Internationalized
Resource Identifiers (IRIs)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_resource_identifier) following [RFC 3987](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986) and [RFC
3986](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3987) defined by the [Internet Engineering Task Force
(IETF)](https://docs.rs/ietf.org) to uniquely identify objects across the web. IRIs are a
superclass of URIs accepting international characters defined in the
[Unicode](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode) table.

URI/IRIs are defined as a sequence of characters with distinguishable components: a scheme, an authority, a path, a query and a fragment.

```
    foo://example.com:8042/over/there?name=ferret#nose
    \_/   \______________/\_________/ \_________/ \__/
     |           |            |            |        |
  scheme     authority       path        query   fragment
```
This crate provides types to represent borrowed and owned URIs and IRIs
(`Uri`, `Iri`, `UriBuf`, `IriBuf`), borrowed and owned URIs and IRIs
references (`UriRef`, `IriRef`, `UriRefBuf`, `IriRefBuf`) and similar
types for every part of an URI/IRI. Theses allows the easy access and
manipulation of every components.
It features:

- borrowed and owned URI/IRIs and URI/IRI-reference;
- mutable URI/IRI buffers (in-place);
- path normalization;
- comparison modulo normalization;
- URI/IRI-reference resolution;
- static URI/IRI parsing using the `uri!``iri!`
- `serde`support (by enabling the- `serde`feature).
- `no_std`support (by disabling the default- `std`feature).

[§](https://docs.rs#basic-usage)Basic usage

You can parse an IRI string slice by simply calling [ Iri::new](https://docs.rs/iri/struct.Iri.html#method.new).
No memory allocation occurs using this function, it only borrows the input
data, and validates it. Access to each component is done in linear time.

```
use iref::Iri;
let iri = Iri::new("https://www.rust-lang.org/foo/bar?query#frag")?;
println!("scheme: {}", iri.scheme());
println!("authority: {}", iri.authority().unwrap());
println!("path: {}", iri.path());
println!("query: {}", iri.query().unwrap());
println!("fragment: {}", iri.fragment().unwrap());
```
IRIs can be created and modified using the `IriBuf` type.
With this type, the IRI is held in a single buffer, modified in-place to
reduce memory allocations and optimize memory accesses.
This also allows the conversion from `IriBuf` into `Iri`.

```
use iref::IriBuf;
let mut iri = IriBuf::new("https://www.rust-lang.org".to_string())?;
iri.authority_mut().unwrap().set_port(Some("40".try_into()?));
iri.set_path("/foo".try_into()?);
iri.path_mut().push("bar".try_into()?);
iri.set_query(Some("query".try_into()?));
iri.set_fragment(Some("fragment".try_into()?));
assert_eq!(iri, "https://www.rust-lang.org:40/foo/bar?query#fragment");
```
The `try_into` method is used to ensure that each string is syntactically
correct (for instance, it is not possible to replace `"query"` with
`"query?"` since `?` is not a valid query character).

[§](https://docs.rs#detailed-usage)Detailed Usage

# lib.rs - source

# iref/lib.rs

[1](https://docs.rs#1)//! This crates provides an implementation of
[2](https://docs.rs#2)//! [Uniform Resource Identifiers (URIs, aka URLs)][uri] and [Internationalized
[3](https://docs.rs#3)//! Resource Identifiers (IRIs)][iri] following [RFC 3987][uri-rfc] and [RFC
[4](https://docs.rs#4)//! 3986][iri-rfc] defined by the [Internet Engineering Task Force
[5](https://docs.rs#5)//! (IETF)][ietf] to uniquely identify objects across the web. IRIs are a
[6](https://docs.rs#6)//! superclass of URIs accepting international characters defined in the
[7](https://docs.rs#7)//! [Unicode][unicode] table.
[8](https://docs.rs#8)//!
[9](https://docs.rs#9)//! [uri]: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uniform_Resource_Identifier>
[10](https://docs.rs#10)//! [uri-rfc]: <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986>
[11](https://docs.rs#11)//! [iri]: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationalized_resource_identifier>
[12](https://docs.rs#12)//! [iri-rfc]: <https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3987>
[13](https://docs.rs#13)//! [ietf]: <ietf.org>
[14](https://docs.rs#14)//! [unicode]: <https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unicode>
[15](https://docs.rs#15)//!
[16](https://docs.rs#16)//! URI/IRIs are defined as a sequence of characters with distinguishable
[17](https://docs.rs#17)//! components: a scheme, an authority, a path, a query and a fragment.
[18](https://docs.rs#18)//!
[19](https://docs.rs#19)//! ```text
[20](https://docs.rs#20)//!     foo://example.com:8042/over/there?name=ferret#nose
[21](https://docs.rs#21)//!     \_/   \______________/\_________/ \_________/ \__/
[22](https://docs.rs#22)//!      |           |            |            |        |
[23](https://docs.rs#23)//!   scheme     authority       path        query   fragment
[24](https://docs.rs#24)//! ```
[25](https://docs.rs#25)//!
[26](https://docs.rs#26)//! This crate provides types to represent borrowed and owned URIs and IRIs
[27](https://docs.rs#27)//! (`Uri`, `Iri`, `UriBuf`, `IriBuf`), borrowed and owned URIs and IRIs
[28](https://docs.rs#28)//! references (`UriRef`, `IriRef`, `UriRefBuf`, `IriRefBuf`) and similar
[29](https://docs.rs#29)//! types for every part of an URI/IRI. Theses allows the easy access and
[30](https://docs.rs#30)//! manipulation of every components.
[31](https://docs.rs#31)//! It features:
[32](https://docs.rs#32)//!   - borrowed and owned URI/IRIs and URI/IRI-reference;
[33](https://docs.rs#33)//!   - mutable URI/IRI buffers (in-place);
[34](https://docs.rs#34)//!   - path normalization;
[35](https://docs.rs#35)//!   - comparison modulo normalization;
[36](https://docs.rs#36)//!   - URI/IRI-reference resolution;
[37](https://docs.rs#37)//!   - static URI/IRI parsing using the [`uri!`]/[`iri!`] macros.
[38](https://docs.rs#38)//!   - `serde` support (by enabling the `serde` feature).
[39](https://docs.rs#39)//!   - `no_std` support (by disabling the default `std` feature).
[40](https://docs.rs#40)//!
[41](https://docs.rs#41)//! ## Basic usage
[42](https://docs.rs#42)//!
[43](https://docs.rs#43)//! You can parse an IRI string slice by simply calling [`Iri::new`].
[44](https://docs.rs#44)//! No memory allocation occurs using this function, it only borrows the input
[45](https://docs.rs#45)//! data, and validates it. Access to each component is done in linear time.
[46](https://docs.rs#46)//!
[47](https://docs.rs#47)//! ```rust
[48](https://docs.rs#48)//! use iref::Iri;
[49](https://docs.rs#49)//!
[50](https://docs.rs#50)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), iref::IriError<&'static str>> {
[51](https://docs.rs#51)//! let iri = Iri::new("https://www.rust-lang.org/foo/bar?query#frag")?;
[52](https://docs.rs#52)//!
[53](https://docs.rs#53)//! println!("scheme: {}", iri.scheme());
[54](https://docs.rs#54)//! println!("authority: {}", iri.authority().unwrap());
[55](https://docs.rs#55)//! println!("path: {}", iri.path());
[56](https://docs.rs#56)//! println!("query: {}", iri.query().unwrap());
[57](https://docs.rs#57)//! println!("fragment: {}", iri.fragment().unwrap());
[58](https://docs.rs#58)//! #
[59](https://docs.rs#59)//! # Ok(())
[60](https://docs.rs#60)//! # }
[61](https://docs.rs#61)//! ```
[62](https://docs.rs#62)//!
[63](https://docs.rs#63)//! IRIs can be created and modified using the `IriBuf` type.
[64](https://docs.rs#64)//! With this type, the IRI is held in a single buffer, modified in-place to
[65](https://docs.rs#65)//! reduce memory allocations and optimize memory accesses.
[66](https://docs.rs#66)//! This also allows the conversion from `IriBuf` into `Iri`.
[67](https://docs.rs#67)//!
[68](https://docs.rs#68)//! ```rust
[69](https://docs.rs#69)//! use iref::IriBuf;
[70](https://docs.rs#70)//!
[71](https://docs.rs#71)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), iref::IriError<std::borrow::Cow<'static, str>>> {
[72](https://docs.rs#72)//! let mut iri = IriBuf::new("https://www.rust-lang.org".to_string())?;
[73](https://docs.rs#73)//!
[74](https://docs.rs#74)//! iri.authority_mut().unwrap().set_port(Some("40".try_into()?));
[75](https://docs.rs#75)//! iri.set_path("/foo".try_into()?);
[76](https://docs.rs#76)//! iri.path_mut().push("bar".try_into()?);
[77](https://docs.rs#77)//! iri.set_query(Some("query".try_into()?));
[78](https://docs.rs#78)//! iri.set_fragment(Some("fragment".try_into()?));
[79](https://docs.rs#79)//!
[80](https://docs.rs#80)//! assert_eq!(iri, "https://www.rust-lang.org:40/foo/bar?query#fragment");
[81](https://docs.rs#81)//! # Ok(())
[82](https://docs.rs#82)//! # }
[83](https://docs.rs#83)//! ```
[84](https://docs.rs#84)//!
[85](https://docs.rs#85)//! The `try_into` method is used to ensure that each string is syntactically
[86](https://docs.rs#86)//! correct (for instance, it is not possible to replace `"query"` with
[87](https://docs.rs#87)//! `"query?"` since `?` is not a valid query character).
[88](https://docs.rs#88)//!
[89](https://docs.rs#89)//! ## Detailed Usage
[90](https://docs.rs#90)//!
[91](https://docs.rs#91)//! ### Path manipulation
[92](https://docs.rs#92)//!
[93](https://docs.rs#93)//! The IRI path is accessed through the `path` or `path_mut` methods.
[94](https://docs.rs#94)//! It is possible to access the segments of a path using the iterator returned
[95](https://docs.rs#95)//! by the `segments` method.
[96](https://docs.rs#96)//!
[97](https://docs.rs#97)//! ```rust
[98](https://docs.rs#98)//! # use iref::Iri;
[99](https://docs.rs#99)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), iref::IriError<&'static str>> {
[100](https://docs.rs#100)//! # let iri = Iri::new("https://www.rust-lang.org/foo/bar?query#frag")?;
[101](https://docs.rs#101)//! for segment in iri.path().segments() {
[102](https://docs.rs#102)//!   println!("{}", segment);
[103](https://docs.rs#103)//! }
[104](https://docs.rs#104)//! # Ok(())
[105](https://docs.rs#105)//! # }
[106](https://docs.rs#106)//! ```
[107](https://docs.rs#107)//!
[108](https://docs.rs#108)//! One can use the `normalized_segments` method to iterate over the normalized
[109](https://docs.rs#109)//! version of the path where dot segments (`.` and `..`) are removed.
[110](https://docs.rs#110)//! In addition, it is possible to push or pop segments to a path using the
[111](https://docs.rs#111)//! corresponding methods:
[112](https://docs.rs#112)//! ```rust
[113](https://docs.rs#113)//! # use iref::IriBuf;
[114](https://docs.rs#114)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), iref::IriError<std::borrow::Cow<'static, str>>> {
[115](https://docs.rs#115)//! let mut iri = IriBuf::new("https://rust-lang.org/a/c".to_string())?;
[116](https://docs.rs#116)//! let mut path = iri.path_mut();
[117](https://docs.rs#117)//!
[118](https://docs.rs#118)//! path.pop();
[119](https://docs.rs#119)//! path.push("b".try_into()?);
[120](https://docs.rs#120)//! path.push("c".try_into()?);
[121](https://docs.rs#121)//! path.push("".try_into()?); // the empty segment is valid.
[122](https://docs.rs#122)//!
[123](https://docs.rs#123)//! assert_eq!(iri.path(), "/a/b/c/");
[124](https://docs.rs#124)//! # Ok(())
[125](https://docs.rs#125)//! # }
[126](https://docs.rs#126)//! ```
[127](https://docs.rs#127)//!
[128](https://docs.rs#128)//! ### IRI references
[129](https://docs.rs#129)//!
[130](https://docs.rs#130)//! This crate provides the two types `IriRef` and `IriRefBuf` to represent
[131](https://docs.rs#131)//! IRI references. An IRI reference is either an IRI or a relative IRI.
[132](https://docs.rs#132)//! Contrarily to regular IRIs, relative IRI references may have no scheme.
[133](https://docs.rs#133)//!
[134](https://docs.rs#134)//! ```rust
[135](https://docs.rs#135)//! # use iref::{Iri, IriRef, IriRefBuf};
[136](https://docs.rs#136)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), iref::IriError<&'static str>> {
[137](https://docs.rs#137)//! let mut iri_ref = IriRefBuf::default(); // an IRI reference can be empty.
[138](https://docs.rs#138)//!
[139](https://docs.rs#139)//! // An IRI reference with a scheme is a valid IRI.
[140](https://docs.rs#140)//! iri_ref.set_scheme(Some("https".try_into()?));
[141](https://docs.rs#141)//! let iri: &Iri = iri_ref.as_iri().unwrap();
[142](https://docs.rs#142)//!
[143](https://docs.rs#143)//! // An IRI can be safely converted into an IRI reference.
[144](https://docs.rs#144)//! let iri_ref: &IriRef = iri.into();
[145](https://docs.rs#145)//! # Ok(())
[146](https://docs.rs#146)//! # }
[147](https://docs.rs#147)//! ```
[148](https://docs.rs#148)//!
[149](https://docs.rs#149)//! Given a base IRI, references can be resolved into a regular IRI using the
[150](https://docs.rs#150)//! [Reference Resolution Algorithm](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986#section-5)
[151](https://docs.rs#151)//! defined in [RFC 3986](https://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc3986).
[152](https://docs.rs#152)//! This crate provides a *strict* implementation of this algorithm.
[153](https://docs.rs#153)//!
[154](https://docs.rs#154)//! ```rust
[155](https://docs.rs#155)//! # use iref::{Iri, IriRef, IriRefBuf};
[156](https://docs.rs#156)//! # fn main() -> Result<(), iref::IriError<::std::borrow::Cow<'static, str>>> {
[157](https://docs.rs#157)//! let base_iri = Iri::new("http://a/b/c/d;p?q")?;
[158](https://docs.rs#158)//! let mut iri_ref = IriRefBuf::new("g;x=1/../y".to_string())?;
[159](https://docs.rs#159)//!
[160](https://docs.rs#160)//! // non mutating resolution.
[161](https://docs.rs#161)//! assert_eq!(iri_ref.resolved(base_iri), "http://a/b/c/y");
[162](https://docs.rs#162)//!
[163](https://docs.rs#163)//! // in-place resolution.
[164](https://docs.rs#164)//! iri_ref.resolve(base_iri);
[165](https://docs.rs#165)//! assert_eq!(iri_ref, "http://a/b/c/y");
[166](https://docs.rs#166)//! # Ok(())
[167](https://docs.rs#167)//! # }
[168](https://docs.rs#168)//! ```
[169](https://docs.rs#169)//!
[170](https://docs.rs#170)//! This crate implements
[171](https://docs.rs#171)//! [Errata 4547](https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/eid4547) about the
[172](https://docs.rs#172)//! abnormal use of dot segments in relative paths.
[173](https://docs.rs#173)//! This means that for instance, the path `a/b/../../../` is normalized into
[174](https://docs.rs#174)//! `../`.
[175](https://docs.rs#175)//!
[176](https://docs.rs#176)//! ### IRI comparison
[177](https://docs.rs#177)//!
[178](https://docs.rs#178)//! Here are the features of the IRI comparison method implemented in this crate.
[179](https://docs.rs#179)//!
[180](https://docs.rs#180)//! #### Protocol agnostic
[181](https://docs.rs#181)//!
[182](https://docs.rs#182)//! This implementation does not know anything about existing protocols.
[183](https://docs.rs#183)//! For instance, even if the
[184](https://docs.rs#184)//! [HTTP protocol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypertext_Transfer_Protocol)
[185](https://docs.rs#185)//! defines `80` as the default port,
[186](https://docs.rs#186)//! the two IRIs `http://example.org` and `http://example.org:80` are **not** equivalent.
[187](https://docs.rs#187)//!
[188](https://docs.rs#188)//! #### Every `/` counts
[189](https://docs.rs#189)//!
[190](https://docs.rs#190)//! The path `/foo/bar` is **not** equivalent to `/foo/bar/`.
[191](https://docs.rs#191)//!
[192](https://docs.rs#192)//! #### Path normalization
[193](https://docs.rs#193)//!
[194](https://docs.rs#194)//! Paths are normalized during comparison by removing dot segments (`.` and `..`).
[195](https://docs.rs#195)//! This means for instance that the paths `a/b/c` and `a/../a/./b/../b/c` **are**
[196](https://docs.rs#196)//! equivalent.
[197](https://docs.rs#197)//! Note however that this crate implements
[198](https://docs.rs#198)//! [Errata 4547](https://www.rfc-editor.org/errata/eid4547) about the
[199](https://docs.rs#199)//! abnormal use of dot segments in relative paths.
[200](https://docs.rs#200)//! This means that for instance, the IRI `http:a/b/../../../` is equivalent to
[201](https://docs.rs#201)//! `http:../` and **not** `http:`.
[202](https://docs.rs#202)//!
[203](https://docs.rs#203)//! #### Percent-encoded characters
[204](https://docs.rs#204)//!
[205](https://docs.rs#205)//! Thanks to the [`pct-str` crate](https://crates.io/crates/pct-str),
[206](https://docs.rs#206)//! percent encoded characters are correctly handled.
[207](https://docs.rs#207)//! The two IRIs `http://example.org` and `http://exa%6dple.org` **are**
[208](https://docs.rs#208)//! equivalent.
[209](https://docs.rs#209)#![cfg_attr(not(feature = "std"), no_std)]

# Iri in iref::iri - Rust

Source: https://docs.rs/iref/4.1.0/iref/iri/struct.Iri.html

`pub struct Iri(/* private fields */);`## Expand description

Uniform Resource Identifier (IRI).

[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use iref::iri::{Iri, Scheme, Authority, Path, Query, Fragment};
let iri = Iri::new("https://www.rust-lang.org/foo/bar?query#fragment")?;
assert_eq!(iri.scheme(), Scheme::new(b"https").unwrap());
assert_eq!(iri.authority(), Some(Authority::new("www.rust-lang.org").unwrap()));
assert_eq!(iri.path(), Path::new("/foo/bar").unwrap());
assert_eq!(iri.query(), Some(Query::new("query").unwrap()));
assert_eq!(iri.fragment(), Some(Fragment::new("fragment").unwrap()));
```

Creates a new IRI by parsing the input bytes.

Creates a new IRI by parsing the input string.

Returns all the parts of this IRI.

This method parses the IRI and returns a [ IriParts](https://docs.rs/struct.IriParts.html) struct containing
references to each component: scheme, authority, path, query, and
fragment.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use iref::Iri;
let iri = Iri::new("https://example.org:8080/path?query#fragment").unwrap();
let parts = iri.parts();
assert_eq!(parts.scheme, "https");
assert_eq!(parts.authority.unwrap(), "example.org:8080");
assert_eq!(parts.path, "/path");
assert_eq!(parts.query.unwrap(), "query");
assert_eq!(parts.fragment.unwrap(), "fragment");
```
The IRI without the file name, query and fragment.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-3)Example

```
let a = Iri::new("https://crates.io/crates/iref?query#fragment").unwrap();
let b = Iri::new("https://crates.io/crates/iref/?query#fragment").unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.base(), "https://crates.io/crates/");
assert_eq!(b.base(), "https://crates.io/crates/iref/")
```
Joins a IRI reference to this IRI, returning a new owned IRI.

This method resolves the given IRI reference against this IRI as a base, following the reference resolution algorithm defined in RFC 3986.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-4)Example

```
use iref::{Iri, IriRef};
let base = Iri::new("https://example.org/foo/bar").unwrap();
let reference = IriRef::new("../baz").unwrap();
assert_eq!(base.joined(reference), "https://example.org/baz");
```

```
use iref::Iri;
let base = Iri::new("https://example.org/foo/bar").unwrap();
assert_eq!(base.try_joined("../baz").unwrap(), "https://example.org/baz");
assert!(base.try_joined("not a valid iri ref\0").is_err());
```

Returns a copy of this IRI with the given scheme.

#### pub fn [parts](https://docs.rs#method.parts-1)(&self) -> [IriRefParts](https://docs.rs/struct.IriRefParts.html)<'_>

Returns all the parts of this IRI reference.

This method parses the IRI reference and returns a [ IriRefParts](https://docs.rs/struct.IriRefParts.html)
struct containing references to each component: scheme, authority, path,
query, and fragment. Unlike

[, the scheme is optional.](https://docs.rs/struct.Iri.html#method.parts)

`Iri::parts`[§](https://docs.rs#example-11)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let iri_ref = IriRef::new("//example.org/path?query#fragment").unwrap();
let parts = iri_ref.parts();
assert!(parts.scheme.is_none());
assert_eq!(parts.authority.unwrap(), "example.org");
assert_eq!(parts.path, "/path");
assert_eq!(parts.query.unwrap(), "query");
assert_eq!(parts.fragment.unwrap(), "fragment");
```

```

#### pub fn [relative_to](https://docs.rs#method.relative_to)(&self, other: &Self) -> [IriRefBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.IriRefBuf.html)

Returns this IRI reference relative to the given base.

Computes a relative IRI reference that, when resolved against `other`,
would produce `self`. This is the inverse operation of resolution.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-25)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let base = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo/bar").unwrap();
let target = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo/baz").unwrap();
assert_eq!(target.relative_to(base), "baz");
let other = IriRef::new("https://example.org/other").unwrap();
assert_eq!(other.relative_to(base), "../other");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iref/opt/rustwide/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/build/iref-5bd578105f42a43f/out/iri.rs.html#4720-4732)

Returns the suffix of this IRI relative to the given prefix.

Returns `Some((suffix, query, fragment))` if this IRI is of the form
`prefix/suffix?query#fragment` where `prefix` is given as parameter.
Returns `None` otherwise.
If the scheme or authority differs from the prefix, returns `None`.

See [ Path::suffix](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html#method.suffix) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-26)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let iri = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo/bar/baz?query").unwrap();
let prefix = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo").unwrap();
let (suffix, query, fragment) = iri.suffix(prefix).unwrap();
assert_eq!(suffix, "bar/baz");
assert_eq!(query.unwrap(), "query");
assert!(fragment.is_none());
```

assert_eq!(b.base(), "https://crates.io/crates/iref/")

1.9.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#374)#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#374)

#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Checks that `index`-th byte is the first byte in a UTF-8 code point
sequence or the end of the string.

The start and end of the string (when `index == self.len()`) are
considered to be boundaries.

Returns `false` if `index` is greater than `self.len()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(0));
// start of `老`
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(6));
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(s.len()));
// second byte of `ö`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(2));
// third byte of `老`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(8));
```
1.91.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#423)#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#423)

#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Finds the closest `x` not exceeding `index` where [ is_char_boundary(x)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.is_char_boundary) is

`true`.This method can help you truncate a string so that it’s still valid UTF-8, but doesn’t exceed a given number of bytes. Note that this is done purely at the character level and can still visually split graphemes, even though the underlying characters aren’t split. For example, the emoji 🧑🔬 (scientist) could be split so that the string only includes 🧑 (person) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let s = "❤️🧡💛💚💙💜";
assert_eq!(s.len(), 26);
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(13));
let closest = s.floor_char_boundary(13);
assert_eq!(closest, 10);
assert_eq!(&s[..closest], "❤️🧡");
```

Converts a string slice to a raw pointer.

As string slices are a slice of bytes, the raw pointer points to a
[ u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html). This pointer will be pointing to the first byte of the string
slice.

The caller must ensure that the returned pointer is never written to.
If you need to mutate the contents of the string slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let s = "Hello";
let ptr = s.as_ptr();
```

This is the non-panicking alternative to indexing the `str`. Returns
[ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) whenever equivalent indexing operation would panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let v = String::from("🗻∈🌏");

// indices not on UTF-8 sequence boundaries

This is the unchecked alternative to indexing the `str`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that these preconditions are satisfied:

- The starting index must not exceed the ending index;
- Indexes must be within bounds of the original slice;
- Indexes must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

Failing that, the returned string slice may reference invalid memory or
violate the invariants communicated by the `str` type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let v = "🗻∈🌏";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("🗻", v.get_unchecked(0..4));
    assert_eq!("∈", v.get_unchecked(4..7));
    assert_eq!("🌏", v.get_unchecked(7..11));
}
```

The argument, `mid`, should be a byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,

and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

Returns an iterator over the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s of a string slice.

As a string slice consists of valid UTF-8, we can iterate through a
string slice by [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html). This method returns such an iterator.

It’s important to remember that [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html) represents a Unicode Scalar
Value, and might not match your idea of what a ‘character’ is. Iteration
over grapheme clusters may be what you actually want. This functionality
is not provided by Rust’s standard library, check crates.io instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

Basic usage:

```

assert_eq!(7, count);
let mut chars = word.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('g'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('d'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('b'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('e'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```
Remember, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s might not match your intuition about characters:

```
let y = "y̆";
let mut chars = y.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next()); // not 'y̆'
assert_eq!(Some('\u{0306}'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```

1.1.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1210)#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1210)

#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

Splits a string slice by whitespace.

The iterator returned will return string slices that are sub-slices of the original string slice, separated by any amount of whitespace.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`. If you only want to split on ASCII whitespace
instead, use [ split_ascii_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_ascii_whitespace).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let mut iter = "A few words".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("A"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("few"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("words"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
All kinds of whitespace are considered:

```
let mut iter = " Mary   had\ta\u{2009}little  \n\t lamb".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("Mary"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("had"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("a"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("little"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("lamb"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
If the string is empty or all whitespace, the iterator yields no string slices:

```
assert_eq!("".split_whitespace().next(), None);
assert_eq!("   ".split_whitespace().next(), None);
```

Returns an iterator over the lines of a string, as string slices.

Lines are split at line endings that are either newlines (`\n`) or
sequences of a carriage return followed by a line feed (`\r\n`).

Line terminators are not included in the lines returned by the iterator.

Note that any carriage return (`\r`) not immediately followed by a
line feed (`\n`) does not split a line. These carriage returns are
thereby included in the produced lines.

The final line ending is optional. A string that ends with a final line ending will return the same lines as an otherwise identical string without a final line ending.

An empty string returns an empty iterator.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let text = "foo\r\nbar\n\nbaz\r";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(Some("foo"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("bar"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some(""), lines.next());
// Trailing carriage return is included in the last line
assert_eq!(Some("baz\r"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(None, lines.next());
```
The final line does not require any ending:

```
let text = "foo\nbar\n\r\nbaz";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(Some("foo"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("bar"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some(""), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("baz"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(None, lines.next());
```
An empty string returns an empty iterator:

```
let text = "";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(lines.next(), None);
```

Returns an iterator over substrings of this string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`If there are no matches the full string slice is returned as the only item in the iterator.

[§](https://docs.rs#iterator-behavior)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator will be a [ DoubleEndedIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/double_ended/trait.DoubleEndedIterator.html) if the pattern
allows a reverse search and forward/reverse search yields the same
elements. This is true for, e.g.,

[, but not for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char``&str`.If the pattern allows a reverse search but its results might differ
from a forward search, the [ rsplit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.rsplit) method can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb".split(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary", "had", "a", "little", "lamb"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".split('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".split('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "", "tiger", "leopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lion::tiger::leopard".split("::").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "tiger", "leopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "AABBCC".split("DD").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["AABBCC"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1def2ghi".split(char::is_numeric).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "def", "ghi"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXtigerXleopard".split(char::is_uppercase).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "tiger", "leopard"]);
```
If the pattern is a slice of chars, split on each occurrence of any of the characters:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "2020-11-03 23:59".split(&['-', ' ', ':', '@'][..]).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["2020", "11", "03", "23", "59"]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1defXghi".split(|c| c == '1' || c == 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "def", "ghi"]);
```
If a string contains multiple contiguous separators, you will end up with empty strings in the output:

```
let x = "||||a||b|c".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split('|').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "", "", "", "a", "", "b", "c"]);
```
Contiguous separators are separated by the empty string.

```
let x = "(///)".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split('/').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["(", "", "", ")"]);
```
Separators at the start or end of a string are neighbored by empty strings.

```
let d: Vec<_> = "010".split("0").collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "1", ""]);
```
When the empty string is used as a separator, it separates every character in the string, along with the beginning and end of the string.

```
let f: Vec<_> = "rust".split("").collect();
assert_eq!(f, &["", "r", "u", "s", "t", ""]);
```
Contiguous separators can lead to possibly surprising behavior when whitespace is used as the separator. This code is correct:

```
let x = "    a  b c".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "", "", "", "a", "", "b", "c"]);
```
It does *not* give you:

Use [ split_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_whitespace) for this behavior.

Differs from the iterator produced by `split` in that `split_inclusive`
leaves the matched part as the terminator of the substring.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

`char`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-25)Examples

```

    .split_inclusive('\n').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary had a little lamb\n", "little lamb\n", "little lamb."]);
```
If the last element of the string is matched, that element will be considered the terminator of the preceding substring. That substring will be the last item returned by the iterator.

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb\nlittle lamb\nlittle lamb.\n"
    .split_inclusive('\n').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary had a little lamb\n", "little lamb\n", "little lamb.\n"]);
```

[§](https://docs.rs#text-directionality)Text directionality

A string is a sequence of bytes. `start` in this context means the first
position of that byte string; for a left-to-right language like English or
Russian, this will be left side, and for right-to-left languages like
Arabic or Hebrew, this will be the right side.

```
let s = "  English  ";
assert!(Some('E') == s.trim_start().chars().next());
let s = "  עברית  ";
assert!(Some('ע') == s.trim_start().chars().next());
```

#### pub fn [trim_right](https://docs.rs#method.trim_right)(&self) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

superseded by `trim_end`

Returns a string slice with trailing whitespace removed.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`.

[§](https://docs.rs#text-directionality-3)Text directionality

A string is a sequence of bytes. ‘Right’ in this context means the last
position of that byte string; for a language like Arabic or Hebrew
which are ‘right to left’ rather than ‘left to right’, this will be
the *left* side, not the right.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-41)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = " Hello\tworld\t";
assert_eq!(" Hello\tworld", s.trim_right());
```
Directionality:

```
let s = "English  ";
assert!(Some('h') == s.trim_right().chars().rev().next());
let s = "עברית  ";
assert!(Some('ת') == s.trim_right().chars().rev().next());
```

#### pub fn [trim_prefix](https://docs.rs#method.trim_prefix)<P>(&self, prefix: P) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

`trim_prefix_suffix`)Returns a string slice with the optional prefix removed.

If the string starts with the pattern `prefix`, returns the substring after the prefix.
Unlike [ strip_prefix](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.strip_prefix), this method always returns

`&str` for easy method chaining,
instead of returning [.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html)

`Option<&str>`If the string does not start with `prefix`, returns the original string unchanged.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-47)Examples

```
#![feature(trim_prefix_suffix)]
// Prefix present - removes it
assert_eq!("foo:bar".trim_prefix("foo:"), "bar");
assert_eq!("foofoo".trim_prefix("foo"), "foo");
// Prefix absent - returns original string
assert_eq!("foo:bar".trim_prefix("bar"), "foo:bar");
// Method chaining example
assert_eq!("<https://example.com/>".trim_prefix('<').trim_suffix('>'), "https://example.com/");
```

Because `parse` is so general, it can cause problems with type
inference. As such, `parse` is one of the few times you’ll see
the syntax affectionately known as the ‘turbofish’: `::<>`. This
helps the inference algorithm understand specifically which type
you’re trying to parse into.

`parse` can parse into any type that implements the [ FromStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Will return [ Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html#associatedtype.Err) if it’s not possible to parse this string slice into
the desired type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-52)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let four: u32 = "4".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(4, four);
```
Using the ‘turbofish’ instead of annotating `four`:

```
let four = "4".parse::<u32>();
assert_eq!(Ok(4), four);
```
Failing to parse:

```
let nope = "j".parse::<u32>();
assert!(nope.is_err());
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#2907)#### pub fn [eq_ignore_case_unnormalized](https://docs.rs#method.eq_ignore_case_unnormalized)(&self, other: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`casefold`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#2907)

#### pub fn [eq_ignore_case_unnormalized](https://docs.rs#method.eq_ignore_case_unnormalized)(&self, other: &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

`casefold`)Checks that two strings are a caseless match, according to
[Definition 144](https://www.unicode.org/versions/latest/core-spec/chapter-3/#G53513) in Chapter 3 of the Unicode Standard.

Same as `a.to_casefold_unnormalized() == b.to_casefold_unnormalized()`,
but without allocating. See that method’s documentation,
as well as [ char::to_casefold_unnormalized()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html#method.to_casefold_unnormalized),
for more information about case folding.

No [normalization](https://www.unicode.org/faq/normalization.html) (e.g. NFC) is performed, so visually and semantically identical strings
might still compare unequal. For example, `"Å"` (U+00C5 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A WITH RING ABOVE)
is considered distinct from `"Å"` (A followed by U+030A COMBINING RING ABOVE),
even though Unicode considers them canonically equivalent.

In addition, this method is independent of language/locale, so the special behavior of I/ı/İ/i in Turkish and Azeri is not handled.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-55)Examples

```
#![feature(casefold)]
assert!("Ferris".eq_ignore_case_unnormalized("FERRIS"));
assert!("Ferrös".eq_ignore_case_unnormalized("FERRÖS"));
assert!("ẞ".eq_ignore_case_unnormalized("ss"));
```
No NFC [normalization](https://www.unicode.org/faq/normalization.html) is performed:

```
#![feature(casefold)]
// These two strings are visually and semantically identical...
let comp = "Å";
let decomp = "Å";
// ... but not codepoint-for-codepoint equal.
assert_eq!(comp, "\u{C5}");
assert_eq!(decomp, "A\u{030A}");
// Their case-foldings are likewise unequal:
assert!(!comp.eq_ignore_case_unnormalized(decomp));
```

Returns `None` if `substr` does not point within `self`.

Unlike [ str::find](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.find),

**this does not search through the string**. Instead, it uses pointer arithmetic to find where in the string

`substr` is derived from.This is useful for extending [ str::split](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split) and similar methods.

Note that this method may return false positives (typically either
`Some(0..0)` or `Some(self.len()..self.len())`) if `substr` is a
zero-length `str` that points at the beginning or end of another,
independent, `str`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-62)Examples

```
use core::range::Range;
let data = "a, b, b, a";
let mut iter = data.split(", ").map(|s| data.substr_range(s).unwrap());
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(Range { start: 0, end: 1 }));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(Range { start: 3, end: 4 }));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(Range { start: 6, end: 7 }));
assert_eq!(iter.next(), Some(Range { start: 9, end: 10 }));
```
Returns the same string as a string slice `&str`.

This method is redundant when used directly on `&str`, but
it helps dereferencing other string-like types to string slices,
for example references to `Box<str>` or `Arc<str>`.

Replaces all matches of a pattern with another string.

`replace` creates a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), and copies the data from this string slice into it.
While doing so, it attempts to find matches of a pattern. If it finds any, it
replaces them with the replacement string slice.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-63)Examples

```
let s = "this is old";
assert_eq!("this is new", s.replace("old", "new"));
assert_eq!("than an old", s.replace("is", "an"));
```
When the pattern doesn’t match, it returns this string slice as [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html):

```
let s = "this is old";
assert_eq!(s, s.replace("cookie monster", "little lamb"));
```
Replaces first N matches of a pattern with another string.

`replacen` creates a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html), and copies the data from this string slice into it.
While doing so, it attempts to find matches of a pattern. If it finds any, it
replaces them with the replacement string slice at most

`count` times.[§](https://docs.rs#examples-64)Examples

```
let s = "foo foo 123 foo";
assert_eq!("new new 123 foo", s.replacen("foo", "new", 2));
assert_eq!("faa fao 123 foo", s.replacen('o', "a", 3));
assert_eq!("foo foo new23 foo", s.replacen(char::is_numeric, "new", 1));
```
When the pattern doesn’t match, it returns this string slice as [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html):

```
let s = "this is old";
assert_eq!(s, s.replacen("cookie monster", "little lamb", 10));
```
1.2.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#433)#### pub fn [to_lowercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_lowercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#433)

#### pub fn [to_lowercase](https://docs.rs#method.to_lowercase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

Returns the lowercase equivalent of this string slice, as a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html).

‘Lowercase’ is defined according to the terms of
[Chapter 3 (Conformance)](https://www.unicode.org/versions/latest/core-spec/chapter-3/#G34432)
of the Unicode standard.

Since some characters can expand into multiple characters when changing
the case, this function returns a [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) instead of modifying the
parameter in-place.

Unlike [ char::to_lowercase()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html#method.to_lowercase), this method fully handles the context-dependent
casing of Greek sigma. However, like that method, it does not handle locale-specific
casing, like Turkish and Azeri I/ı/İ/i. See its documentation
for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-65)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let s = "HELLO WORLD";
assert_eq!("hello world", s.to_lowercase());
```
Tricky examples, with sigma:

```
let sigma = "Σ";
assert_eq!("σ", sigma.to_lowercase());
// but at the end of a word, it's ς, not σ:
let odysseus = "ὈΔΥΣΣΕΎΣ";
assert_eq!("ὀδυσσεύς", odysseus.to_lowercase());
let odysseus_king_of_ithaca = "Ο ΟΔΥΣΣΈΑΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΆΣ ΤΗΣ ΙΘΆΚΗΣ";
assert_eq!("ο οδυσσέας βασιλιάς της ιθάκης", odysseus_king_of_ithaca.to_lowercase());
```
Languages without case are not changed:

```
let new_year = "农历新年";
assert_eq!(new_year, new_year.to_lowercase());
```
[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#554)#### pub fn [word_to_titlecase](https://docs.rs#method.word_to_titlecase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`titlecase`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#554)

#### pub fn [word_to_titlecase](https://docs.rs#method.word_to_titlecase)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`titlecase`)Returns the titlecase equivalent of this string slice,
which is assumed to represent a single word,
as a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html).

Essentially, this consists of uppercasing the first cased letter
(with [ char::to_titlecase()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html#method.to_titlecase)), and lowercasing everything that follows.

‘Titlecase’ is defined according to the terms of
[Chapter 3 (Conformance)](https://www.unicode.org/versions/latest/core-spec/chapter-3/#G34082)
of the Unicode standard.

Since some characters can expand into multiple characters when changing
the case, this function returns a [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) instead of modifying the
parameter in-place.

Unlike [ char::to_lowercase()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html#method.to_lowercase), this method fully handles the context-dependent
casing of Greek sigma. However, like that method, it does not handle locale-specific
casing, like Turkish and Azeri I/ı/İ/i. See its documentation
for more information.

This method does not perform any kind of word segmentation.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-66)Examples

Basic usage:

```
#![feature(titlecase)]
let s = "HELLO WORLD";
assert_eq!("Hello world", s.word_to_titlecase());
```
The first *cased* letter is uppercased:

```
#![feature(titlecase)]
let the_night_before_christmas = "'twas";
assert_eq!("'Twas", the_night_before_christmas.word_to_titlecase());
```
Languages without case are not changed:

```
#![feature(titlecase)]
let new_year = "农历新年";
assert_eq!(new_year, new_year.word_to_titlecase());
```
Georgian uppercase (“Mtavruli”) letters are not used in titlecase:

```
#![feature(titlecase)]
let georgian = "ერთობაშია";
assert_eq!(georgian, georgian.word_to_titlecase());
```
No word segmentation is performed, so only the first cased letter in the whole string gets uppercased:

```
#![feature(titlecase)]
let blazingly_fast = "ferris and I";
assert_eq!("Ferris and i", blazingly_fast.word_to_titlecase());
```
Tricky examples, with sigma:

```
#![feature(titlecase)]
let odysseus = "ὈΔΥΣΣΕΎΣ";
assert_eq!("Ὀδυσσεύς", odysseus.word_to_titlecase());
let odysseus_king_of_ithaca = "Ο ΟΔΥΣΣΈΑΣ ΒΑΣΙΛΙΆΣ ΤΗΣ ΙΘΆΚΗΣ";
assert_eq!("Ο οδυσσέας βασιλιάς της ιθάκης", odysseus_king_of_ithaca.word_to_titlecase());
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#742)#### pub fn [to_casefold_unnormalized](https://docs.rs#method.to_casefold_unnormalized)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`casefold`)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/alloc/str.rs.html#742)

#### pub fn [to_casefold_unnormalized](https://docs.rs#method.to_casefold_unnormalized)(&self) -> [String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html)

`casefold`)Returns the case-folded equivalent of this string slice, as a new [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html).

Case folding is a transformation, mostly matching lowercase, that is meant to be used for case-insensitive string comparisons. Case-folded strings should not usually be exposed directly to users.

For the precise specification of case folding, see
[Chapter 3 (Conformance)](https://www.unicode.org/versions/latest/core-spec/chapter-3/#G63737)
of the Unicode standard.

Since some characters can expand into multiple characters when case folding,
this function returns a [ String](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/alloc/string/struct.String.html) instead of modifying the parameter in-place.

No [normalization](https://www.unicode.org/faq/normalization.html) (e.g. NFC) is performed, so visually and semantically identical strings
might still casefold differently. For example, `"Å"` (U+00C5 LATIN CAPITAL LETTER A WITH RING ABOVE)
is considered distinct from `"Å"` (A followed by U+030A COMBINING RING ABOVE),
even though Unicode considers them canonically equivalent.

Like [ char::to_casefold_unnormalized()](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html#method.to_casefold_unnormalized) this method does not handle language-specific
casing, like Turkish and Azeri I/ı/İ/i. See that method’s documentation
for more information.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-68)Examples

Basic usage:

```
#![feature(casefold)]
let s0 = "HELLO";
let s1 = "Hello";
assert_eq!(s0.to_casefold_unnormalized(), s1.to_casefold_unnormalized());
assert_eq!(s0.to_casefold_unnormalized(), "hello")
```
Scripts without case are not changed:

```
#![feature(casefold)]
let new_year = "农历新年";
assert_eq!(new_year, new_year.to_casefold_unnormalized());
```
One character can become multiple:

```
#![feature(casefold)]
let s0 = "TSCHÜẞ";
let s1 = "TSCHÜSS";
let s2 = "tschüß";
assert_eq!(s0.to_casefold_unnormalized(), s1.to_casefold_unnormalized());
assert_eq!(s0.to_casefold_unnormalized(), s2.to_casefold_unnormalized());
assert_eq!(s0.to_casefold_unnormalized(), "tschüss");
```
No NFC [normalization](https://www.unicode.org/faq/normalization.html) is performed:

```
#![feature(casefold)]
// These two strings are visually and semantically identical...
let comp = "Å";
let decomp = "Å";
// ... but not codepoint-for-codepoint equal.
assert_eq!(comp, "\u{C5}");
assert_eq!(decomp, "A\u{030A}");
// Their case-foldings are likewise unequal:
assert_eq!(comp.to_casefold_unnormalized(), "\u{E5}");
assert_eq!(decomp.to_casefold_unnormalized(), "a\u{030A}");
```

#### pub fn [parts](https://docs.rs#method.parts)(&self) -> [IriRefParts](https://docs.rs/struct.IriRefParts.html)<'_>

Returns all the parts of this IRI reference.

This method parses the IRI reference and returns a [ IriRefParts](https://docs.rs/struct.IriRefParts.html)
struct containing references to each component: scheme, authority, path,
query, and fragment. Unlike

[, the scheme is optional.](https://docs.rs/struct.Iri.html#method.parts)

`Iri::parts`[§](https://docs.rs#example)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let iri_ref = IriRef::new("//example.org/path?query#fragment").unwrap();
let parts = iri_ref.parts();
assert!(parts.scheme.is_none());
assert_eq!(parts.authority.unwrap(), "example.org");
assert_eq!(parts.path, "/path");
assert_eq!(parts.query.unwrap(), "query");
assert_eq!(parts.fragment.unwrap(), "fragment");
```
Returns the scheme of the IRI reference, if any.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-1)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let absolute = IriRef::new("https://example.org/path").unwrap();
assert_eq!(absolute.scheme().unwrap(), "https");
let relative = IriRef::new("/path").unwrap();
assert!(relative.scheme().is_none());
```

#### pub fn [without_fragment](https://docs.rs#method.without_fragment)(&self) -> &Self

Returns this IRI reference without the fragment component.

If the IRI reference has a fragment (e.g. `#section`), it is removed
along with the `#` delimiter. If there is no fragment, the original
IRI reference is returned unchanged.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-12)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let iri_ref = IriRef::new("https://example.org/path?query#frag").unwrap();
assert_eq!(iri_ref.without_fragment(), "https://example.org/path?query");
let no_frag = IriRef::new("https://example.org/path").unwrap();
assert_eq!(no_frag.without_fragment(), "https://example.org/path");
```

#### pub fn [without_query_and_fragment](https://docs.rs#method.without_query_and_fragment)(&self) -> &Self

Returns this IRI reference without the query and fragment components.

If the IRI reference has a query (e.g. `?key=value`) or fragment
(e.g. `#section`), they are removed along with their delimiters.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-13)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let iri_ref = IriRef::new("https://example.org/path?query#frag").unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    iri_ref.without_query_and_fragment(),
    "https://example.org/path"
);
let no_query = IriRef::new("https://example.org/path#frag").unwrap();
assert_eq!(
    no_query.without_query_and_fragment(),
    "https://example.org/path"
);
```

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iref/opt/rustwide/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/build/iref-5bd578105f42a43f/out/iri.rs.html#4635-4694)

#### pub fn [relative_to](https://docs.rs#method.relative_to)(&self, other: &Self) -> [IriRefBuf](https://docs.rs/struct.IriRefBuf.html)

Returns this IRI reference relative to the given base.

Computes a relative IRI reference that, when resolved against `other`,
would produce `self`. This is the inverse operation of resolution.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-14)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let base = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo/bar").unwrap();
let target = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo/baz").unwrap();
assert_eq!(target.relative_to(base), "baz");
let other = IriRef::new("https://example.org/other").unwrap();
assert_eq!(other.relative_to(base), "../other");
```
[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iref/opt/rustwide/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/build/iref-5bd578105f42a43f/out/iri.rs.html#4720-4732)

[Source](https://docs.rs/src/iref/opt/rustwide/target/x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu/debug/build/iref-5bd578105f42a43f/out/iri.rs.html#4720-4732)

Returns the suffix of this IRI relative to the given prefix.

Returns `Some((suffix, query, fragment))` if this IRI is of the form
`prefix/suffix?query#fragment` where `prefix` is given as parameter.
Returns `None` otherwise.
If the scheme or authority differs from the prefix, returns `None`.

See [ Path::suffix](https://docs.rs/struct.Path.html#method.suffix) for more details.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-15)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let iri = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo/bar/baz?query").unwrap();
let prefix = IriRef::new("https://example.org/foo").unwrap();
let (suffix, query, fragment) = iri.suffix(prefix).unwrap();
assert_eq!(suffix, "bar/baz");
assert_eq!(query.unwrap(), "query");
assert!(fragment.is_none());
```
The IRI reference without the file name, query and fragment.

[§](https://docs.rs#example-16)Example

```
let a = IriRef::new("https://crates.io/crates/iref?query#fragment").unwrap();
let b = IriRef::new("https://crates.io/crates/iref/?query#fragment").unwrap();
assert_eq!(a.base(), "https://crates.io/crates/");
assert_eq!(b.base(), "https://crates.io/crates/iref/")
```
Returns this IRI reference as a IRI, if it has a scheme.

A IRI reference with a scheme is a valid IRI.
Returns `None` if this is a relative reference (no scheme).

[§](https://docs.rs#example-17)Example

```
use iref::IriRef;
let absolute = IriRef::new("https://example.org/path").unwrap();
assert!(absolute.as_iri().is_some());
let relative = IriRef::new("/path").unwrap();
assert!(relative.as_iri().is_none());
```

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#374)

#### pub fn [is_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.is_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [bool](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.bool.html)

Checks that `index`-th byte is the first byte in a UTF-8 code point
sequence or the end of the string.

The start and end of the string (when `index == self.len()`) are
considered to be boundaries.

Returns `false` if `index` is greater than `self.len()`.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-2)Examples

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(0));
// start of `老`
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(6));
assert!(s.is_char_boundary(s.len()));
// second byte of `ö`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(2));
// third byte of `老`
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(8));
```
1.91.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#423)#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#423)

#### pub fn [floor_char_boundary](https://docs.rs#method.floor_char_boundary)(&self, index: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)

Finds the closest `x` not exceeding `index` where [ is_char_boundary(x)](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.is_char_boundary) is

`true`.This method can help you truncate a string so that it’s still valid UTF-8, but doesn’t exceed a given number of bytes. Note that this is done purely at the character level and can still visually split graphemes, even though the underlying characters aren’t split. For example, the emoji 🧑🔬 (scientist) could be split so that the string only includes 🧑 (person) instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-3)Examples

```
let s = "❤️🧡💛💚💙💜";
assert_eq!(s.len(), 26);
assert!(!s.is_char_boundary(13));
let closest = s.floor_char_boundary(13);
assert_eq!(closest, 10);
assert_eq!(&s[..closest], "❤️🧡");
```

Converts a string slice to a raw pointer.

As string slices are a slice of bytes, the raw pointer points to a
[ u8](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.u8.html). This pointer will be pointing to the first byte of the string
slice.

The caller must ensure that the returned pointer is never written to.
If you need to mutate the contents of the string slice, use [ as_mut_ptr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.as_mut_ptr).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-6)Examples

```
let s = "Hello";
let ptr = s.as_ptr();
```
Returns a subslice of `str`.

This is the non-panicking alternative to indexing the `str`. Returns
[ None](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/option/enum.Option.html#variant.None) whenever equivalent indexing operation would panic.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-7)Examples

```
let v = String::from("🗻∈🌏");
assert_eq!(Some("🗻"), v.get(0..4));
// indices not on UTF-8 sequence boundaries
assert!(v.get(1..).is_none());
assert!(v.get(..8).is_none());
// out of bounds
assert!(v.get(..42).is_none());
```

#### pub unsafe fn [get_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.get_unchecked)<I>(&self, i: I) -> &<I as [SliceIndex](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html)<[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)>>::[Output](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/slice/index/trait.SliceIndex.html#associatedtype.Output)

Returns an unchecked subslice of `str`.

This is the unchecked alternative to indexing the `str`.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-2)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that these preconditions are satisfied:

- The starting index must not exceed the ending index;
- Indexes must be within bounds of the original slice;
- Indexes must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

Failing that, the returned string slice may reference invalid memory or
violate the invariants communicated by the `str` type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-8)Examples

```
let v = "🗻∈🌏";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("🗻", v.get_unchecked(0..4));
    assert_eq!("∈", v.get_unchecked(4..7));
    assert_eq!("🌏", v.get_unchecked(7..11));
}
```

#### pub unsafe fn [slice_unchecked](https://docs.rs#method.slice_unchecked)(&self, begin: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html), end: [usize](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.usize.html)) -> &[str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html)

Creates a string slice from another string slice, bypassing safety checks.

This is generally not recommended, use with caution! For a safe
alternative see [ str](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html) and

[.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/ops/index/trait.Index.html)

`Index`This new slice goes from `begin` to `end`, including `begin` but
excluding `end`.

To get a mutable string slice instead, see the
[ slice_mut_unchecked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.slice_mut_unchecked) method.

[§](https://docs.rs#safety-3)Safety

Callers of this function are responsible that three preconditions are satisfied:

- `begin`must not exceed- `end`.
- `begin`and- `end`must be byte positions within the string slice.
- `begin`and- `end`must lie on UTF-8 sequence boundaries.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-9)Examples

```
let s = "Löwe 老虎 Léopard";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("Löwe 老虎 Léopard", s.slice_unchecked(0, 21));
}
let s = "Hello, world!";
unsafe {
    assert_eq!("world", s.slice_unchecked(7, 12));
}
```
Divides one string slice into two at an index.

The argument, `mid`, should be a byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,
and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

To get mutable string slices instead, see the [ split_at_mut](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_mut)
method.

[§](https://docs.rs#panics)Panics

Panics if `mid` is not on a UTF-8 code point boundary, or if it is past
the end of the last code point of the string slice.  For a non-panicking
alternative see [ split_at_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_checked).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-10)Examples

```
let s = "Per Martin-Löf";
let (first, last) = s.split_at(3);
assert_eq!("Per", first);
assert_eq!(" Martin-Löf", last);
```
Divides one string slice into two at an index.

The argument, `mid`, should be a valid byte offset from the start of the
string. It must also be on the boundary of a UTF-8 code point. The
method returns `None` if that’s not the case.

The two slices returned go from the start of the string slice to `mid`,
and from `mid` to the end of the string slice.

To get mutable string slices instead, see the [ split_at_mut_checked](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_at_mut_checked)
method.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-11)Examples

```
let s = "Per Martin-Löf";
let (first, last) = s.split_at_checked(3).unwrap();
assert_eq!("Per", first);
assert_eq!(" Martin-Löf", last);
assert_eq!(None, s.split_at_checked(13));  // Inside “ö”
assert_eq!(None, s.split_at_checked(16));  // Beyond the string length
```
Returns an iterator over the [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s of a string slice.

As a string slice consists of valid UTF-8, we can iterate through a
string slice by [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html). This method returns such an iterator.

It’s important to remember that [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html) represents a Unicode Scalar
Value, and might not match your idea of what a ‘character’ is. Iteration
over grapheme clusters may be what you actually want. This functionality
is not provided by Rust’s standard library, check crates.io instead.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-12)Examples

Basic usage:

```

assert_eq!(7, count);

assert_eq!(Some('g'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('o'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('d'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('b'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(Some('e'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```
Remember, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)s might not match your intuition about characters:

```
let y = "y̆";
let mut chars = y.chars();
assert_eq!(Some('y'), chars.next()); // not 'y̆'
assert_eq!(Some('\u{0306}'), chars.next());
assert_eq!(None, chars.next());
```

1.1.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1210)#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1210)

#### pub fn [split_whitespace](https://docs.rs#method.split_whitespace)(&self) -> [SplitWhitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitWhitespace.html)<'_>

Splits a string slice by whitespace.

The iterator returned will return string slices that are sub-slices of the original string slice, separated by any amount of whitespace.

‘Whitespace’ is defined according to the terms of the Unicode Derived
Core Property `White_Space`. If you only want to split on ASCII whitespace
instead, use [ split_ascii_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_ascii_whitespace).

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-15)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let mut iter = "A few words".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("A"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("few"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("words"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
All kinds of whitespace are considered:

```
let mut iter = " Mary   had\ta\u{2009}little  \n\t lamb".split_whitespace();
assert_eq!(Some("Mary"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("had"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("a"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("little"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(Some("lamb"), iter.next());
assert_eq!(None, iter.next());
```
If the string is empty or all whitespace, the iterator yields no string slices:

```
assert_eq!("".split_whitespace().next(), None);
assert_eq!("   ".split_whitespace().next(), None);
```

Returns an iterator over the lines of a string, as string slices.

Lines are split at line endings that are either newlines (`\n`) or
sequences of a carriage return followed by a line feed (`\r\n`).

Line terminators are not included in the lines returned by the iterator.

Note that any carriage return (`\r`) not immediately followed by a
line feed (`\n`) does not split a line. These carriage returns are
thereby included in the produced lines.

The final line ending is optional. A string that ends with a final line ending will return the same lines as an otherwise identical string without a final line ending.

An empty string returns an empty iterator.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-17)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let text = "foo\r\nbar\n\nbaz\r";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(Some("foo"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("bar"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some(""), lines.next());
// Trailing carriage return is included in the last line
assert_eq!(Some("baz\r"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(None, lines.next());
```
The final line does not require any ending:

```
let text = "foo\nbar\n\r\nbaz";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(Some("foo"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("bar"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some(""), lines.next());
assert_eq!(Some("baz"), lines.next());
assert_eq!(None, lines.next());
```
An empty string returns an empty iterator:

```
let text = "";
let mut lines = text.lines();
assert_eq!(lines.next(), None);
```

Returns an iterator over substrings of this string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`If there are no matches the full string slice is returned as the only item in the iterator.

[§](https://docs.rs#iterator-behavior)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator will be a [ DoubleEndedIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/double_ended/trait.DoubleEndedIterator.html) if the pattern
allows a reverse search and forward/reverse search yields the same
elements. This is true for, e.g.,

[, but not for](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char``&str`.If the pattern allows a reverse search but its results might differ
from a forward search, the [ rsplit](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.rsplit) method can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-24)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb".split(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary", "had", "a", "little", "lamb"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".split('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".split('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "", "tiger", "leopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lion::tiger::leopard".split("::").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "tiger", "leopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "AABBCC".split("DD").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["AABBCC"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1def2ghi".split(char::is_numeric).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "def", "ghi"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXtigerXleopard".split(char::is_uppercase).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "tiger", "leopard"]);
```
If the pattern is a slice of chars, split on each occurrence of any of the characters:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "2020-11-03 23:59".split(&['-', ' ', ':', '@'][..]).collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["2020", "11", "03", "23", "59"]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1defXghi".split(|c| c == '1' || c == 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "def", "ghi"]);
```
If a string contains multiple contiguous separators, you will end up with empty strings in the output:

```
let x = "||||a||b|c".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split('|').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "", "", "", "a", "", "b", "c"]);
```
Contiguous separators are separated by the empty string.

```
let x = "(///)".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split('/').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["(", "", "", ")"]);
```
Separators at the start or end of a string are neighbored by empty strings.

```
let d: Vec<_> = "010".split("0").collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "1", ""]);
```
When the empty string is used as a separator, it separates every character in the string, along with the beginning and end of the string.

```
let f: Vec<_> = "rust".split("").collect();
assert_eq!(f, &["", "r", "u", "s", "t", ""]);
```
Contiguous separators can lead to possibly surprising behavior when whitespace is used as the separator. This code is correct:

```
let x = "    a  b c".to_string();
let d: Vec<_> = x.split(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(d, &["", "", "", "", "a", "", "b", "c"]);
```
It does *not* give you:

Use [ split_whitespace](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split_whitespace) for this behavior.

1.51.0 · [Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1711)#### pub fn [split_inclusive](https://docs.rs#method.split_inclusive)<P>(&self, pat: P) -> [SplitInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitInclusive.html)<'_, P>

[Source](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/src/core/str/mod.rs.html#1711)

#### pub fn [split_inclusive](https://docs.rs#method.split_inclusive)<P>(&self, pat: P) -> [SplitInclusive](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/iter/struct.SplitInclusive.html)<'_, P>

Returns an iterator over substrings of this string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern.

Differs from the iterator produced by `split` in that `split_inclusive`
leaves the matched part as the terminator of the substring.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://docs.rs#examples-25)Examples

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb\nlittle lamb\nlittle lamb."
    .split_inclusive('\n').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary had a little lamb\n", "little lamb\n", "little lamb."]);
```
If the last element of the string is matched, that element will be considered the terminator of the preceding substring. That substring will be the last item returned by the iterator.

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb\nlittle lamb\nlittle lamb.\n"
    .split_inclusive('\n').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary had a little lamb\n", "little lamb\n", "little lamb.\n"]);
```
Returns an iterator over substrings of the given string slice, separated by characters matched by a pattern and yielded in reverse order.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://docs.rs#iterator-behavior-1)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator requires that the pattern supports a reverse
search, and it will be a [ DoubleEndedIterator](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/iter/traits/double_ended/trait.DoubleEndedIterator.html) if a forward/reverse
search yields the same elements.

For iterating from the front, the [ split](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.split) method can be used.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-26)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lamb".rsplit(' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lamb", "little", "a", "had", "Mary"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".rsplit('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".rsplit('X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["leopard", "tiger", "", "lion"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lion::tiger::leopard".rsplit("::").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["leopard", "tiger", "lion"]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```

Returns an iterator over substrings of the given string slice, separated
by a pattern, restricted to returning at most `n` items.

If `n` substrings are returned, the last substring (the `n`th substring)
will contain the remainder of the string.

The [pattern](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/pattern/index.html) can be a `&str`, [ char](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html), a slice of

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://docs.rs#iterator-behavior-4)Iterator behavior

The returned iterator will not be double ended, because it is not efficient to support.

If the pattern allows a reverse search, the [ rsplitn](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.str.html#method.rsplitn) method can be
used.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-29)Examples

Simple patterns:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "Mary had a little lambda".splitn(3, ' ').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["Mary", "had", "a little lambda"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "lionXXtigerXleopard".splitn(3, "X").collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["lion", "", "tigerXleopard"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "abcXdef".splitn(1, 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abcXdef"]);
let v: Vec<&str> = "".splitn(1, 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, [""]);
```
A more complex pattern, using a closure:

```
let v: Vec<&str> = "abc1defXghi".splitn(2, |c| c == '1' || c == 'X').collect();
assert_eq!(v, ["abc", "defXghi"]);
```

most `n` items.

[s, or a function or closure that determines if a character matches.](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/std/primitive.char.html)

`char`[§](https://docs.rs#iterator-behavior-5)Iterator behavior

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-30)Examples

Simple patterns:

```

Because `parse` is so general, it can cause problems with type
inference. As such, `parse` is one of the few times you’ll see
the syntax affectionately known as the ‘turbofish’: `::<>`. This
helps the inference algorithm understand specifically which type
you’re trying to parse into.

`parse` can parse into any type that implements the [ FromStr](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html) trait.

[§](https://docs.rs#errors)Errors

Will return [ Err](https://doc.rust-lang.org/nightly/core/str/traits/trait.FromStr.html#associatedtype.Err) if it’s not possible to parse this string slice into
the desired type.

[§](https://docs.rs#examples-52)Examples

Basic usage:

```
let four: u32 = "4".parse().unwrap();
assert_eq!(4, four);
```
Using the ‘turbofish’ instead of annotating `four`:

```
let four = "4".parse::<u32>();
assert_eq!(Ok(4), four);
```
Failing to parse:

```
let nope = "j".parse::<u32>();
assert!(nope.is_err());
```
